text.p: Commodity markets mostly opted for caution on Thursday with speculators again selling gold, on a view that it can't offer any early return.
New York precious metals futures ended mostly lower Thursday, led by a further slide in gold to new three year lows, on rumors of more central bank sales.

COMEX April gold ended down $5.70 an ounce at $347.50, after seeing a new contract low at $347.30. Estimated total gold futures volume was a high 61,000 contracts, with contract lows seen in all active delivery months out to February 1998.
Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted at $345.35/85, a new three-year low, compared with the London Thursday afternoon fix at $349.25, and the New York close Wednesday at $351.00/50.
But short term implied lease rates rose sharply Thursday also, suggesting more speculative shorting was occurring in the bullion market, analysts said.

In London, several dealers said they suspected central bank selling was behind the latest decline. Fresh institutional selling had come into the market in early trading, mimicking a similar move on Wednesday morning.

Copper business remained volatile during Thursday afternoon LME trading, with the market whipping under $2,150 at one stage only to unlock some buying and end with pared loosses. Traders said the dip under $2,150 represented a good buying opportunity, while would-be fresh sellers were deterred by the backwardation, which although narrower again today, has the potential to flare up any time. Last three months business was at $2,160, down $23, but above the year's low of $2,142.

The aluminium market threatened to break lower at one stage today, but was ably defended, as expected, between $1,600 and $1,610. By the conclusion of the kerb prices were back at $1,614, little changed from the overnight $1,613.

Nickel prices were resilient this afternoon, with the general level of physical interest seen as reasonable, while consumer expectations of further price falls may be unfounded, traders said. Last kerb trade was at $7,295, up $115 from yesterday.

Zinc was aided by the U.S Mint tender, where the 2,964 tonnes of SHG metal was bought at an average price that was in excess of 5.50 cents/lb over LME cash. Prices concluded the kerb at $1,135, up $9 from the previous close.

Lead staged a mini-rally from yesterday's 15-month lows, and managed to claw above the $670 level. Last trade was at $674, up $4. Tin similarly mounted a modest recovery, helped by late covering, and closed the kerb at $5,820, against a previous $5,800. Alloy edged up in slow trading, and finished $15 higher at $1,505 a tonne.

WHEAT - CBOT wheat futures closed lower on a sharp break in the neighboring soy complex with skepticism that India soon will buy much more wheat on the world market also cited, traders said. The lower close in wheat futures occurred despite a respectable sales tally in the latest USDA export sales report. USDA early Thursday said U.S. net export sales of wheat the week ended January 23 totaled 422,900 tonnes, above expectations for 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes. Wheat futures closed unchanged to 2-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with March unchanged at $3.70-1/4. July was down 1-1/2 at $3.45-1/4.

NYMEX crude oil finished 40 cents higher at $24.87 a barrel despite news the U.N. Secretary General said he expected the oil-for-food deal with Iraq to be renewed another six months in June. Countering the prospect of increased crude supply from Iraq was news that two of Mexico's largest crude ports remained shut for a third day on Thursday as a cold front continued to bring winds of about 50 km per hour to the area, port officials said.
